# Autoplay Transition Pause Migration Checks

This record originally had a very narrow entry point: the old investigation material mentioned autoplay transition pause, then directed readers to `src/types/modules/autoplay.d.ts`. The entry point was not wrong, but too much weight was placed on it. A type file can help locate names, parameter ownership, and adjacent declarations; it is not itself evidence of the runtime pause sequence. Subsequent checks still start here so that the old records remain traceable, not so that every implementation judgment rests on a single `.d.ts` file.

The current checks center on the usable artifacts from the previous round. The description in SWP-209 requires updating only jobs or pinned versions that have actually changed, and this restriction should remain in the migration steps: unchanged items must not be rewritten just because they were "reviewed along the way"; items that can no longer be matched to old artifacts must not have their gaps filled with results borrowed from elsewhere either.

```text
Previous approach
Issue name / call name ──────────────> autoplay.d.ts ─────> Directly assess pause behavior

Revised approach
Issue name / call name ──> autoplay.d.ts ──> References in the same revision ──> Compatibility-related caller records
                                      │
                                      └── Cannot verify: leave unconfirmed, do not change the pinned version
```

## How to Retain the Entry Point

In `v_prev` of `internal/swiper-core`, the old record points to `src/types/modules/autoplay.d.ts`. The direct type adjacency visible at the top of the file is:

```ts
import type Swiper from '../swiper-class.d.ts';
```

This import line only shows that the autoplay type module is adjacent to the `Swiper` type declaration. It does not show that a transition has ended, nor whether pause has already executed or has not yet executed. When reading, first classify this information under "declaration relationships", and do not mix it into "behavior reviewed". The search terms used in the old records can still be used: `interaction`, `autoplay`, `transition`, `pause`, `while`, `waitfortransition`, `pauseonmouseenter`, `paused`. These terms are clues for recovering the old context, not a set of conditions that must all hold at the same location.

Two kinds of lookup are easily confused.

- Looking up the declaration file from the issue name provides a location clue. It answers "which module the old record is roughly associated with".
- Continuing from the declaration file to inspect references in the same revision is what may reveal a call relationship. It answers "whether a compatibility-related caller goes through this entry point, and which item should remain in the current checks".

If the second kind leads nowhere, do not go back and state the first kind more definitively. In particular, do not treat the type import of `Swiper` as shorthand for the autoplay runtime chain. The earlier draft documented only this adjacency, and this is precisely the gap it left.

## What Is Being Migrated from the Old Records

The migration is not about files, nor is it about replacing one path with another; what is being migrated is the undifferentiated judgments in the old investigation records. The old material may have put an issue name, a call name, a declaration entry point, and an artifact result in the same sentence. The new records need to separate them so that a later change to one pinned version does not inadvertently change the meaning at another level.

First organize the information in the following suggested order, with the option to stop after any individual step:

1. Retain the object name `autoplay transition pause` written in the old material, and note that it is the search entry point for this round of compatibility checks.
2. Open `src/types/modules/autoplay.d.ts`, and extract only the declaration locations and direct type adjacency relevant to the current issue. The currently confirmed adjacency is the `Swiper` type import.
3. Continue checking references within the same revision. Record whether a reference consumes the declaration, passes an object, or only imposes type constraints; if no reference is found, record "not found" rather than supplying a runtime explanation for it.
4. Compare against the usable artifacts from the previous round, and list the jobs or pinned versions that actually need to be checked again. Include only items that have changed.
5. Keep entries that still cannot be linked to references or artifacts separately. They can continue to block closure of the checks, but must not be marked as fully migrated.

Here, the "usable artifacts from the previous round" are the baseline to restore to, not a new round of conclusions. When comparing, first state clearly which job or pinned version is being compared, then state whether it has changed. If the material does not show a change, do not create an "updated" record. The practical benefit is that when a reference cannot be located, it is still possible to restore the old artifacts; when a pinned version is found to have changed, callers that only pass through the type entry point but are not involved in this round's differences will not be changed by mistake.

## Record Format for Compatibility-Related Callers

There is no need to collect callers into a long list on this page. A short paragraph is enough for each caller actually involved in this round of checks: which entry point was used to find it, how it relates to `autoplay.d.ts`, which job or pinned version was compared, and whether the result is confirmed or unconfirmed. This preserves the old path without misrepresenting the new path as the location of the implementation.

Additional notes can use the following format:

| Item | What to write |
| --- | --- |
| Location source | Issue name or call name in the old record |
| Declaration entry point | `src/types/modules/autoplay.d.ts` |
| Visible adjacency | `import type Swiper from '../swiper-class.d.ts';` |
| Further checks | References in the same revision, and the corresponding compatibility-related callers |
| Artifact comparison | List only jobs or pinned versions that have actually changed |
| Current status | Confirmed / Still unconfirmed |

Do not use "Current status" in the table as a substitute for observations. For example, an entry marked "still unconfirmed" must at least record where progress is blocked: whether only the declaration entry point was found, or a caller was found but there is not yet a corresponding artifact comparison. Conversely, "confirmed" should also point back to a specific reference or changed item, rather than being assumed valid just because the title contains pause.

## Handling the Old Wording

The initial draft tended to treat `autoplay.d.ts` as the center of the compatibility checks. That wording is retained as a historical entry point, but is no longer a completion criterion. The completion criteria are now narrower: the object referenced by the old record can be located again; jobs or pinned versions that actually changed can be compared against the usable artifacts from the previous round; areas still missing references or results are explicitly left open.

This does not mean redoing all related modules every time. For unchanged jobs or pinned versions, continue using the usable artifacts from the previous round; for information already confirmed to be only type adjacency, retain it only for navigation; only information that has actually changed and can be traced to a caller belongs in this round's update. Putting all three in the same checklist may seem convenient, but it would leave readers unable to distinguish the old baseline from the current changes.

When restoring the old path, first revert to the usable artifacts from the previous round, then move the records added in this round from "confirmed" back to "pending verification". Do not delete the old issue names or declaration entry points: they remain the starting points for locating things next time. What needs to be withdrawn is the newly added judgments that lack supporting references or artifact comparisons, not the old entry point itself.

## Status After This Round of Review

SWP-209 still has one unconfirmed point, so it cannot be treated as complete. This status has nothing to do with whether the type entry point exists: the entry point has been available throughout, and what remains unconfirmed is whether enough corresponding links have been established when following the entry point through to references, compatibility-related callers, and artifact differences. When adding information later, prioritize filling this gap rather than merely appending more autoplay keywords.

If the review finds that a job or pinned version has actually changed, the updated record should also retain its correspondence with the usable artifacts from the previous round; if it only finds that the terms in the old record are still adjacent to the current declarations, leave the finding at the declaration level. Both outcomes can reduce repeated searching next time, but they cannot substitute for each other.

For experiments related to controller loop repair, see DOC-22 separately; the controller check results are not merged here. The two pages can share lookup entry points during the release, but should not combine unconfirmed items for different objects into the same pause assessment.

## Notes Still to Be Added

- Which compatibility-related callers can be located by following references to `src/types/modules/autoplay.d.ts` still needs to be documented using the revision from that time.
- When adding notes, state clearly whether unconfirmed items are blocked at reference relationships or artifact comparison, rather than just changing the status.
- If a pinned version changes but the job does not, the existing material has not yet concluded whether a comparison should be listed separately.

# History of clickable class

The entry point noted in May is still there, but "start at the declaration" was later misread as "the declaration owns the implementation." These two judgments need to be kept separate. The first only anchors the investigation to something we can recheck; the second already assigns responsibility for runtime behavior. There wasn't enough evidence at the time to support the second claim.

When we revisited `src/types/modules/pagination.d.ts` in September, the immediate type relationships shown in the file were limited:

```ts

```

They are useful for answering "what types are used to express the configuration fields" and "what type context the pagination object sits in," not for answering when a token is written to DOM. The old conclusion has not been deleted, because it does explain why the initial investigation stopped here; from this revision onward, it is no longer taken as establishing implementation ownership.

**Use the pagination declaration as the terminology anchor, then check the example and the actual execution path separately.** This requires one extra turn in the investigation, but puts "how fields are named" and "what was seen on the page" in different columns. We decided on this approach.

The record therefore starts by separating the objects under review into three layers:

| Location | Responsibility recognized in this record |
| --- | --- |
| `pagination.d.ts` | Provide pagination-related types and a starting point for reading |
| Example results | Record whether the class seen on the page matches expectations |
| Execution path | Explain where the configuration is ultimately consumed; still to be verified |

This table is not a team responsibility matrix. It is only meant to prevent the next investigation from collapsing these three questions back into "there's a problem with clickable class." A review that stops at the type file can confirm fields and immediate type relationships; one that reaches the example can confirm the display difference; only with the actual execution steps is it possible to determine whether the two are directly related.

The earlier inclination was to interpret the import of `Swiper` as "pagination logic directly controls clicks." That inference is now withdrawn. The type import puts the pagination definition in Swiper's type context; it does not guarantee runtime call order. We are retaining this retraction because the earlier search route via `Swiper` leads here, and readers could easily follow the same route to the same conclusion again.

Current decision: Keep `src/types/modules/pagination.d.ts` as the terminology entry point; do not declare runtime ownership of clickable class here. Two items are still missing: whether the class in the example is a configured value, a default value, or some other element state, and which workflow should handle failures in the actual execution steps.

# History of clickable class

This page originally only pinned an easily confused term near pagination. It was later referenced repeatedly, not because the full path of clickable class had already been traced at the time, but because earlier investigations all followed the same name and call clues back to `src/types/modules/pagination.d.ts`. This entry remains useful: readers can first see pagination's type context. But after the entry was reused repeatedly, it also carried forward a premature attribution.

> Old wording: clickable class belongs in the pagination declaration file.

Do not remove this sentence. It records May's working hypothesis, not a conclusion that can now be used as a basis for changing the implementation. At the time, the requirement term, pagination object, and similar class wording appeared together, so the declaration file was first treated as the place to close the investigation. This approach made terminology checking easier, but did not distinguish between "declaring a configuration," "a sample displaying a result," and "the runtime consuming that configuration." When someone later came in through the old link, they would often combine these three things again.

The May decision was actually very narrow: the investigation started from the pagination declaration, but the class seen in the sample was not automatically attributed to this file. That version left two gaps: who turns the configuration into a class on the page, and which execution step the sample result actually corresponds to.

At the time, these two gaps looked like the same problem. Looking back now, their entry points are different. The former requires a record of actual execution; the latter requires a result that can be matched to the sample. What the declaration file can provide is something else: how the pagination object is described at the type level. Treating it as the common answer to all three types of question was this page's earliest mistake.

The old record still contains the sentence "Change the types first to validate the sample." This no longer applies. A type change can alter the interface representation, but cannot by itself establish that a token has appeared or disappeared on the page. It is retained because this is exactly why the investigation once started from the declaration file; after removing it, the old investigation path would look as though it began without reason at an `.d.ts` file.

When revisiting `src/types/modules/pagination.d.ts` in September, the only adjacent items directly visible were two type imports:

```ts
import type { CSSSelector } from '../shared.d.ts';
import type Swiper from '../swiper-class.d.ts';
```

`CSSSelector` lets the relevant pagination fields use selector types; `Swiper` places the pagination definition in Swiper's type context. This describes the file's local responsibilities. It is enough to support "this is a review point for field and type relationships," but not enough to support "this is responsible for adding clickable class to elements."

The September review did not expand this small matter into a large proposal; it only compared three ways of writing it:

| Wording | Benefit at the time | Final handling |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Write it entirely as a sample anomaly | The page result can be followed directly | Not adopted, or the source of the configuration term would be lost |
| Make the declaration file the sole owner | Shortest search path | Rejected, because it would misstate a type description as runtime behavior |
| Record the declaration, sample, and execution steps separately | Each location has its own verification target | Adopted, acknowledging that the execution chain is not yet complete |

The second option was rejected, not because the type file is unimportant, but because it cannot answer when the token appears. The third does not mean turning one question into three unrelated documents. The file path, sample result, and execution steps can point to one another, but cannot replace one another. Seeing `clickable` and immediately changing the types, or looking only at a sample difference and declaring the interface definition wrong, were both shortcuts to avoid at the time.

The September version therefore changed the reading order to three categories of objects: `pagination.d.ts` retains the field and type adjacency; the sample side records what actually appeared on the page; the execution side explains through which steps the configuration is consumed. Without execution-side material, do not assign an implementation owner to the token's write location. Here, "owner" refers only to the attribution that needs to be confirmed in this investigation, not to a team responsibility inferred from the type imports.

In particular, one cannot infer the click-handling path from `Swiper`'s type-only import. It explains the type context in which the pagination definition is located, but cannot say who receives clicks or when clickable class changes. The old document once used this clue to imply that the main class owned the behavior; that implication has now been withdrawn. The original paragraph remains so that readers coming from the old search entry can see the correction, rather than reading the import relationship as a call relationship.

From October onward, SWP-211 re-grounded this boundary in the actual evidence. The observation recorded when the card was created was that the actual entry point for clickable class did not match the sample result. Once the card entered the processing stage, it requested a review, requiring the build logs to be traced to find the step where "clickable class tokens" actually execute, and to fill in the corresponding workflow and fallback entry point.

This is not evidence that "the type declaration is wrong." It only shows that the previously omitted execution side needs to be investigated. If the logs show that the relevant configuration was not consumed by the actual step, changing the types will not resolve the sample discrepancy; if the step has already consumed the configuration but the result still differs, the sample input and page state must also be checked. These two cases require different materials, so one cannot choose a fix first and then work backward to justify it.

For now, the current verification relationships are retained as shown below. The arrows indicate objects that still need to be checked during review; they do not indicate confirmed runtime calls:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  state "pagination type review" as types
  state "sample result check" as sample
  state "build log execution step" as execution
  state "workflow and fallback entry point" as workflow
  [*] --> types
  types --> sample: when the sample is inconsistent
  sample --> execution: check the actual step
  execution --> workflow: to be filled in
```

This diagram also explains why the old entry was not deprecated. When an interface review only needs to confirm field wording, stopping at the first item is reasonable; when a sample discrepancy appears, going directly from the sample to the build logs is also reasonable. What must not happen is skipping the intermediate material: seeing the declaration and declaring runtime ownership, or seeing the page result and declaring the interface definition wrong.

The local decision still in effect is as follows. `src/types/modules/pagination.d.ts` remains the terminology and interface-review entry point for clickable class; its maintenance scope is the type description of pagination and the adjacent type relationships. The actual execution step for clickable class tokens, the workflow that handles it, and the fallback entry point should be confirmed separately using the build logs indicated by SWP-211. The existing materials provide neither a verifiable workflow name nor a specific fallback action, so this page does not fill in a seemingly complete ownership.

The requirement term itself is still related to pagination, but "related" can no longer be written as "implementation ownership." A token may be allowed in a configuration and observed in a sample; the two need not come from the same location. In May, because selectors needed to be expressed in the pagination type, it was inferred that clickable class would be handled along the same path; this inference was not supported. Selector types are part of the field representation and cannot replace checking the nodes, sample rendering, or click process.

Two old approaches were not continued. The first was to list all possible class names here and put them back into the pagination configuration one by one; the existing materials do not contain a sufficient token list, and writing it this way would instead make people think that this page already covered the sample and execution sides. The second was to write the handling of SWP-211 directly as an interface-change decision; the card asks us to first find the actual execution step and does not conclude that the interface needs to change. Both approaches remain documented as branches from that time, but are no longer current actions.

Still to be confirmed: the actual execution step corresponding to "clickable class tokens" in the build logs; which workflow handles that step and where the fallback entry point is; whether there is a directly verifiable correspondence between the sample result and the configuration fields; and, among the records in the old search that only hit `pagination.d.ts`, which ones were checking the interface and which ones were checking runtime behavior.

The page remains in place because the old links and issue name will still bring people here. After opening it, readers should be able to distinguish that the declaration file is a reliable terminology entry point, but not a complete explanation of clickable class behavior.

# Troubleshooting Boolean Module Properties

This runbook covers cases where type diagnostics, initialization results, or subsequent control behavior do not match expectations when a module property is set to a boolean. First, retain the caller's original configuration, the version actually in use, and the reproduction environment. Don't replace a boolean with an object just because you see a type issue.

Start at `src/types/swiper-class.d.ts`. This is a class-related TypeScript declaration file. Its header shows type dependencies on `SwiperOptions`, `CSSSelector`, `SwiperModule`, `SwiperEvents`, and `A11yMethods`. If a parameter name or value shape is unclear, continue tracing back from `SwiperOptions`, then return to the actual call site.

```text
Module configuration is a boolean
├─ Editor or compiler reports a type issue
│  └─ Check the parameter name at the call site against the declaration in SwiperOptions
└─ Type checking passes, but behavior is unexpected after initialization
   └─ Check the value's source before creation and writes after initialization
```

If the value comes from a variable, record its source before creation; if the configuration goes through object merging, check the last object to overwrite that property. Type diagnostics disappearing does not mean initialization is working again. In particular, don't end the investigation just because you've replaced the original snippet with an empty object.

We haven't confirmed a specific caller or whether different modules share the same handling path. Review records must include at least the call entry point, property name and value, version, environment, and CI job; if any item is missing, stop at that gap. Do not infer runtime results from the declaration file.

# Troubleshooting Boolean Module Properties

This page starts with an actual configuration, rather than the name of a type file. After a caller sets module properties to boolean values, problems may appear in the editor, or they may not surface until after instance initialization. Record these two types of symptoms separately: for the former, first check the parameter declarations; for the latter, first check whether the values change before and after entering the creation entry point.

The file currently available for direct reference is `src/types/swiper-class.d.ts`. The repository index identifies it as an existing ts module, suitable for reading the code and checking historical behavior. It is not a runtime entry point that can explain initialization results on its own. The following direct dependencies are visible at the top of the file:

- `import type { SwiperOptions } from './swiper-options.d.ts';`
- `import type { CSSSelector, SwiperModule } from './shared.d.ts';`
- `import type { SwiperEvents } from './swiper-events.d.ts';`
- `import type { A11yMethods } from './modules/a11y.d.ts';`

`SwiperOptions` is the next stop for parameter definitions; `CSSSelector`, `SwiperModule`, `SwiperEvents` and `A11yMethods` show that the class declarations also connect to shared types, event types and module method types. These import relationships only indicate where to read next. They cannot, on their own, prove that a boolean input has been handled, nor can they replace a check of the caller.

## Start with the symptoms, not with changing values

There are usually two starting points in an actual case. The first is that the editor or compilation stage already reports an inconsistency in a module property: in this case, the problem may be the property name, object nesting level or value shape. The second is that type checking passes, but the module does not exhibit the expected behavior after the instance is created: in this case, trace where the value came from before creation, and whether there are any explicit writes or control actions after initialization. Collapsing these two symptoms into "boolean values are not supported" loses the actual branches.

First, copy the configuration snippet as actually written by the caller. Preserve the property name, `true` or `false`, adjacent parameters in the same object and the entry point used to create the instance. Simply writing "module enabled" or "module disabled" is not enough, because that loses the property's nesting level within the object and cannot distinguish between module parameters, instance fields and control values after initialization.

If the value comes from a variable, record where the variable is produced before creation; if it comes from a conditional expression, record the branch actually taken; if the configuration goes through an object merge, preserve the order of the objects involved before and after the merge. There is no need to bring in the entire caller here, but the snippet must show whether the boolean value was replaced, and which object ultimately enters the creation entry point.

Environment fields must accompany the snippet as well. The actual version used, the reproduction environment and the CI job are all required. With different versions, the type declarations and initialization paths may differ; with different environments, observations after initialization may fall under different control branches; the CI job is used to distinguish locally observed messages from the actual rejection point in the pipeline. If any of these items is missing, record the gap, and do not fill it in with results from another set.

```text
Module boolean parameter found
│
├─ Is a call snippet available?
│  ├─ No: Leave pending until the call entry point is found
│  └─ Yes: Record the property name, value, creation entry point, version, environment, CI job
│
├─ Is there a type mismatch in the editor or at compile time?
│  ├─ Yes: Follow the declarations and parameter names branch
│  └─ No: Follow the before/after initialization branch
│
└─ Does the behavior occur only after initialization?
   ├─ Yes: Look for explicit writes or control code after initialization
   └─ No: Do not attribute the cause to the class declaration at this stage
```

"A call snippet is available" does not mean the cause is already known. At a minimum, you also need to know who creates the instance, which item in the object is a boolean, and whether the object is merged or replaced before creation. If any of these three pieces of information is missing, stop the investigation at the missing piece, and do not fill in the runtime result using a type name seen in a declaration file.

## What the declaration-file step can answer

If the editor or compilation has already flagged a mismatch, start with `SwiperOptions`. First, copy the full property name used by the caller, not just `true` or `false`. Second, locate the property with the same name, or the closest level, in the parameter type. Third, distinguish whether the difference is in the property name, the shape of the value, or the object's nesting level. Finally, return to the call site and check whether this value is overwritten by a conditional expression, a default value, or an object merge before it is passed in.

If you cannot find the parameter name, first check whether it has been placed at the wrong configuration level. The module object may be placed at the top level or inside another parameter object; when the same field text appears at different levels, the type hints do not point to the same thing. In this case, do not describe the issue as "booleans are not supported", because the actual mismatch may be in the property name or the object's location.

If the parameter with the same name can be located but the shape of the value is still unclear, record the result as "Type entry point found, value semantics pending confirmation from the caller". Do not interpret the import of `SwiperModule` as meaning that the module has been registered, and do not interpret the presence of `CSSSelector` as meaning that a selector has taken effect. The current file provides declaration adjacency, not a call stack from an execution.

There is another situation that is easy to confuse: the search results first lead to a class declaration file, so it is assumed to be where the boolean configuration is handled. This judgment can only explain why the search starts here, and cannot serve as a basis for changing the caller. What you actually need to trace is the parameter name used by the caller, the shape of the value passed in, and the creation entry point.

If you find a similar field in `SwiperOptions`, you must still distinguish "declaration found" from "input has been accepted". A declaration can show what the type checker is comparing, but it cannot tell you whether the object ultimately received by the creation entry point still retains that field. After the field has gone through merging, default values, or conditional expressions, you must return to the call site and review it again.

If someone directly replaces the boolean value with an empty object, the disappearance of the type diagnostic only shows that the new input more closely matches the current declaration. It does not explain why the original input appeared, nor does it show that the initialization result has been restored. When a comparison is needed, the original snippet must be retained, and the replacement object can only be used as a separate sample, with a note stating which version, environment, and CI job produced the result. If no object sample is available, do not fabricate an object just to complete the comparison.

## Where the value comes from before creation

When type checking passes, first shift your attention away from the declaration files. Focus on where the boolean value comes from and what form it ultimately takes when it reaches the creation entry point. If a constant is written directly at the call site, retain that configuration and the adjacent fields; if a variable is passed at the call site, trace it back to where it is generated; if objects are merged at the call site, record the object that last overwrites that property.

If a modification occurs before creation, first check where it is made. At this point, the initialization result cannot yet be attributed to the configuration snippet the caller initially saw, nor can you assume that the final object retains the original value just because it still contains a property with the same name. Record the value before the modification, the value after the modification, and the final state entering the creation entry point; if any one of these is missing, mark it as unconfirmed.

Object merging is especially likely to obscure this distinction. Seeing `true` in the original configuration does not mean that the creation entry point still receives `true`; a later object may overwrite that property, or it may only add adjacent fields. Recording the merge order is more useful than recording a final statement that "the module is true", because the order determines which value actually remains.

If the value comes from a conditional expression, do not just copy the expression itself. Record which branch was actually selected in the reproduction environment, and retain the other branch that was not taken as context. If two environments take different branches, the local type-checking result and the CI result cannot be directly combined into a single sample.

If you confirm that no replacement was found before the configuration reaches the creation entry point, that only means the original value was seen within the scope reviewed so far. It does not mean that the module has already processed it in a particular way, much less that all modules accept the same boolean form. Further assessment must look at whether there are any explicit writes or control actions after initialization.

```text
Original configuration found
├─ Modified before creation
│  └─ Check where the modification occurs first, do not attribute it to initialization yet
├─ Original value reaches the creation entry point
│  ├─ Explicit write after initialization
│  │  └─ Compare before and after the write, then examine the observed result
│  └─ No explicit write found
│     └─ Continue reading along the actual creation entry point
└─ Cannot confirm whether the original value reaches the entry point
   └─ Fill in the value source or object merge order
```

"No subsequent write found" and "There is no subsequent write" are not the same thing. The former only means that none was located within the current search scope, while the latter requires sufficient coverage of the call scope. If the configuration snippet is incomplete, only the former wording can be used. Do not close off this branch just because you do not immediately see a second assignment after initialization.

## How to record observations after initialization

When an abnormality appears after initialization, first distinguish the observed result from the operations that actually occurred. Just because something happens after creation does not mean that there must have been a second write; finding a piece of control code does not mean that it changed the current module's parameters. In the record, keep "what was observed" separate from "which write was found".

If you find an explicit write, retain the values before and after the write, the write location, and the observed changes. If the write occurs through a control interface, record the entry point actually used by the caller, and do not replace the control interface name with the generic term "runtime update". If you only see an anomaly after instance initialization and have not found a write, continue investigating from the actual call entry point, and keep the declaration file as a reference for type navigation.

There is a practical boundary to this investigation: declaration files can provide a starting point for confirming parameter names and value shapes, but cannot by themselves tell you which module branch was executed after initialization. If the symptom is abnormal control behavior, at a minimum, record the creation entry point, the observation point after initialization, and the existing write locations separately; if any one of these has not been located, do not attribute the symptom to `src/types/swiper-class.d.ts`.

If the configuration reaches the creation entry point unchanged and no explicit write is found after initialization, the result can stop at "The creation entry point and observed results have been retained, the runtime path still needs review". This does not rule out runtime behavior, but accurately describes the material currently available. When there is no caller, no environment, or no CI job, do not use a passing local type check as a substitute for initialization results either.

For each comparison of a boolean sample and an object sample, change only the shape of the module parameter. Only by keeping the other neighboring parameters, creation entry point, version, and environment the same can you tell whether the observed difference comes from this change. If both samples pass type checking but produce different results, return to the creation entry point and the post-initialization code; if only one sample shows a type mismatch, prioritize recording the differences in parameter types and call snippets.

Do not bring in other fixes while making the comparison. If you adjust neighboring parameters, the version, or the initialization order while replacing the boolean sample with an object, the result only shows the difference produced by the entire set of changes, not what the object shape itself changed. If no sample can keep the other conditions unchanged, record the comparison as incomplete rather than choosing the side that looks more stable.

## Previous judgments retained during review

Early notes treated `swiper-class.d.ts` as the first place where boolean module properties are handled. This judgment is retained in the historical context because the filename, Swiper class declaration, and type imports do indeed direct the search here. After review, it was narrowed to: this file is a starting point for tracing back type- and class-related declarations, and `SwiperOptions` is an adjacent point for locating parameter definitions; whether a particular boolean input is handled must be confirmed by returning to the caller and the initialization path.

Early notes also tended to change boolean values into objects whenever they appeared. This action might stop the editor from showing a warning, but it did not explain the original input or indicate which fields the object should contain. Now, if you want to try the object form, you must retain the original call snippet and label the object form as a comparison sample. Comparison results alone cannot serve as a recovery action.

This old action must not be assumed to have succeeded just because "the types are now correct". Passing type checking only means that no further type discrepancies of the same kind were reported at that stage; it does not cover behavior after initialization, nor does it cover another version or another environment. When the version, environment, and CI job do not match, the old judgment can only serve as the working hypothesis at the time and cannot be combined with the new samples into a single conclusion.

There was also a misunderstanding of scope: `SwiperEvents` and `A11yMethods` appeared near the same declaration file, so the investigation was at one point extended to events or accessibility methods. When there are no event-related symptoms, do not investigate event code; when there are no records of method calls, do not infer module behavior from method types. These type dependencies only help identify the area adjacent to the file.

The first draft placed "the type entry point has been found" too close to "runtime behavior has been confirmed". The two must be kept separate during review. The type entry point tells you where to look up parameter names and value shapes; runtime verification tells you what was passed at the call site, whether it was rewritten before creation, and whether there were any writes after initialization. If supporting material is missing for any item, the conclusion for that item must remain unconfirmed.

The earlier assessment can still explain why historical searches first landed on the declaration file, but it cannot determine the current fix. The purpose of retaining the old paragraphs is to let later readers know that a navigation location was mistaken for a processing location at the time; the new investigation records must make clear which local assessment alone they changed, and that they did not establish compatibility across all modules.

## What to leave at the end of a branch

Investigation results should not merely say "checked", but must be tied to specific branches:

- **Parameter name or nesting level mismatch**: Retain the call snippet and the location actually found in `SwiperOptions`; change only the location where a mismatch has been confirmed.
- **Rewritten before creation**: Record the rewrite location, the values before and after the rewrite, and the final value passed to the creation entry point; continue from the rewrite location.
- **The original value reaches the creation entry point, and a confirmed write occurs after initialization**: Record the values before and after the write and the observed changes; do not attribute the result to the declaration file.
- **The original value reaches the creation entry point, and no confirmed write has been found**: Retain the creation entry point and observation results, and verify along the actual runtime path.
- **Caller or environment information is incomplete**: Stop at gathering the missing material; do not submit a speculative change from a boolean to an object.

"Types are fine" is not a complete result either. At a minimum, state whether this was observed in the editor, during compilation, or in a particular CI job; "initialization is normal" must likewise state the entry point and environment where the observation was made. If the passing status comes from CI, record the node where the failure or pass occurred, rather than posting only an overall status. For local observations, retain the environment description; they cannot automatically replace pipeline results.

Failing nodes must also be recorded alongside the commands. Posting only the overall CI status does not show whether the rejection occurred during type checking, the build, or initialization-related tests; posting only the command does not show the environment in which it produced the result. If only one of these is visible, explicitly state that the other has not yet been obtained; do not turn "not observed" into "did not occur".

When the version, environment, and CI job do not match, first record them separately. Do not combine declaration results from one version with runtime results from another into a single conclusion; do not describe a local pass and a CI failure as "intermittent" either. Their differences can be compared only when both sets of conditions are clear.

## Handoff records

Anyone continuing the search for the caller needs at least the following fields:

| Item | What to retain |
| --- | --- |
| Call entry point | Where the instance is created, or local context that can locate it |
| Original configuration | Property names, Boolean values, adjacent parameters and object hierarchy |
| Type path | Whether the parameter was located through `SwiperOptions`, and at which level the difference occurs |
| Value source | The variable, conditional expression or object merge the value comes from |
| Initialization | Whether the original value reaches the creation entry point, and whether there are any explicit subsequent writes |
| Result | What was actually observed, without substituting speculation |
| Conditions | Version, environment and CI job |
| Evidence location | Command, failing node or local location that allows a return to the original context |

"Type path" cannot simply say "normal". It can say "A parameter with the same name was found, but the value's shape still needs to be confirmed", or "The property name at the call site could not be located at the expected level". "Initialization" cannot simply say "reviewed"; it must specify whether the value was rewritten before creation, passed in unchanged, written after initialization, or has not yet been confirmed.

If no caller has been found yet, the handoff can be reduced to two parts: the confirmed entry point `src/types/swiper-class.d.ts`, and the call configuration that still needs to be located. In this case, do not treat shared type imports as investigation findings; they only help the next reader navigate from the class declaration to `SwiperOptions` or related type definitions. Without a caller, do not fill in a speculative module name, object field or runtime result.

If the caller turns out to come from another project or an inaccessible environment, first retain the issue and the handoff location; do not treat configuration samples from a neighboring project as samples for this investigation. The current material only confirms the declaration entry point `swiper-core` and its adjacent types; determining whether other projects use Boolean values in the same way requires their own call snippets.

## Stop points and rerun conditions

It is appropriate to stop this investigation at any of the following points: there is no actual call snippet; the call snippet lacks a version, environment or CI job; the object merge order cannot be confirmed; only post-initialization behavior is visible and the corresponding write has not been found; or runtime behavior can only be inferred from declaration files. At the stop point, state exactly which item is missing; do not cover every gap with "Needs further confirmation".

If the command or failing node has been retained but the call snippet has not, stop at the call entry point; if the call snippet and version are both available but the environment is missing, stop at the reproduction conditions; if all three are available but there is still only post-initialization behavior, stop at the actual write or control entry point. This way, the next review will know which part needs to be filled in, rather than rereading the declaration file from the beginning.

Conversely, the corresponding branch can only be closed when the call entry point, original properties and values, and object states before and after creation are available, and the observations can be tied to the version, environment and CI job. # Breakpoint loop migration verification

This page preserves an old compatibility verification path. It did not originally start from runtime logs, but from the issue name "breakpoint loop migration" and several call names: it first landed on `src/types/swiper-class.d.ts`, then attempted to determine whether the declaration layer could support the behavioral explanation that followed. During later review, the path itself was not deleted, but the scope of what it could prove was narrowed.

## The old route retained for now

The old paragraph follows and is still kept here because someone may use it to find the entry point:

> Starting from the issue name or call name, go to `src/types/swiper-class.d.ts` and search for `loop`, `grid`, `breakpoint`, `changes`, `setbreakpoint`, `params`, and `loopcreate`. After finding the corresponding declarations, continue along the type references to examine the relationship between breakpoint and loop.

The advantage of this approach is that it is fast. The file is an existing ts module, and the index places it under code reading and historical behavior verification; when checking the compatibility issue in R12.4, there is no need to first guess the name of a runtime file. It also explains why old investigation records pointed the issue name and call names here.

However, "finding the declaration" was once casually treated as "finding the execution relationship." This step was later retained as an outdated assessment, rather than continuing to treat it as a conclusion. The adjacency relationships in `swiper-class.d.ts` can help readers confirm the type entry point, but cannot independently replace implementation-side verification.

## What the path looks like after migration

```text
Old entry
Issue name / call name
      |
      v
src/types/swiper-class.d.ts
      |
      v
See loop, breakpoint, or method name

Entry after review
Issue name / call name
      |
      v
src/types/swiper-class.d.ts
      |
      +--> First record the declaration containing the field, event, or parameter
      +--> Then follow the type import at the file header to distinguish adjacent objects
      +--> Only then determine whether there is enough material to continue tracing the implementation
```

Here, "migration" mainly means migration of the verification method: the entry file was not switched to a confirmed runtime implementation file. What changed was the reading order; what was retained was the file entry. If the record contains only names such as `setbreakpoint` or `loopcreate`, first treat them as locator terms; do not write out the caller, execution timing, or loop reconstruction result based on the names alone.

## File boundaries

The direct dependencies currently visible on the frozen path are:

```ts
import type { SwiperOptions } from './swiper-options.d.ts';
import type { CSSSelector, SwiperModule } from './shared.d.ts';
import type { SwiperEvents } from './swiper-events.d.ts';
import type { A11yMethods } from './modules/a11y.d.ts';
```

These four import groups are the local clues that should be retained during review. `SwiperOptions` is useful for confirming where the parameter declaration originates; `CSSSelector` and `SwiperModule` indicate that the file is also connected to shared types and module declarations; `SwiperEvents` is the event-side adjacency; and `A11yMethods` is a specific edge of the module method declaration. These are the relationships visible at the file header; they are not expanded into the complete breakpoint loop dependency graph.

Therefore, the operation sequence is deliberately narrow:

1. Use the issue name or call name to find the file entry for this page.
2. In `src/types/swiper-class.d.ts`, record the matched field, event, parameter, or method name. Do not just copy one search term; copy the declaration context in which it appears.
3. Perform one adjacency check along the direct type import, separately marking which side the options, shared types, events, and module methods belong to.
4. Place the names from the old record alongside these declaration locations. When a name matches, that only indicates successful locating; when it still does not match, retain the name and the unresolved question.
5. Only after obtaining implementation-side material should you add the execution assessment between breakpoint changes and loop behavior. This record does not provide that implementation-side material, so do not add it here.

The first round can cover only steps 1 through 3. This is the work the old draft actually handled; there is no need to pretend the latter two steps were completed just to "close things out."

## How to record compatibility callers

There is no frozen caller list for this review. A call name can lead someone to the declaration file, but cannot prove which framework wrapper, module parameter, or specific component actually consumes this item. When recording a caller, at minimum retain the object name corresponding to it on the declaration side; include it in the migration record only when both the object and the reference can be matched in the revision that was current at the time.

If only `params` is seen, record it as a parameter entry; if `changes` is seen, initially record it as a declaration clue related to the change; if `loopcreate` is seen, record it as a method-name clue. Do not automatically chain the three into the complete sentence "the loop-creation call occurs after the parameter changes." That order can only be confirmed with implementation or test material.

This is also the difference between the old path and the new path: the old path treated a search hit as an explanation of the next step, while the new path separates the hit location from the evidence type. For compatibility callers, the result may still be only a partial record awaiting follow-up, not proof that the migration batch has been completed.

## Audit trail for the two verification rounds

The first round reused the issue name and call name to trace back to the file, producing the file location, search terms, and direct imports. The first round did not establish specific call relationships; the old draft did not state this clearly enough, making it easy for readers to interpret "landing on the declaration file" as "completing the compatibility determination." This does not change the old entry; it only draws the boundary in subsequent records.

The review round continued using the same file but added one action: putting the hit term back into the declaration context, then examining the type objects it connects to. The review did not yield a new conclusion about implementation behavior, so it did not rewrite the old guess as a new definitive statement. The new content that can be confirmed is the checking order and the file-header adjacency; the parts that cannot be confirmed remain as they were.

If records of this kind are processed in batches in the future, the first batch should first clean up the entry: whether the issue name, call name, and file path can all lead back to the same location. The second batch should then handle object relationships: whether parameters, events, and module methods have corresponding declarations and references. The two batches cannot be combined into a single "migration complete"; at present, this page has a complete trace of the first batch and a partial review of the second batch.

## Where to fall back when it fails

If the new verification method cannot find the original hit location, first fall back to the old process: use the original issue name or call name to reopen `src/types/swiper-class.d.ts`, retaining the term and context that matched at the time. Do not jump directly to a guessed runtime entry, and do not delete the old `v_prev` path. Falling back to the old path only means restoring the location; it does not mean that the old assessment is valid again.

If `breakpoint`, `loop`, or `grid` is seen in the declaration file but the corresponding execution material cannot be found, stop at the declaration layer. You may leave "implementation-side follow-up needed," but you cannot use type adjacency as a substitute for the call chain. If only one item is found, record only that item; do not fill in missing fields, methods, or callers just to make before/after look symmetrical.

## Old wording that may still mislead readers

This page previously described "pointing from the issue name and call names to the file" as if it were a complete migration route. That wording is now suitable only as an explanation of the old entry. It does not prove the actual location of changes to breakpoint loop, nor the execution order among `setbreakpoint`, `loopcreate`, and `params`. The old text is not deleted because it still explains why historical searches landed on this file; when using it, read it as a locating record.

The entry point still available for further verification is `src/types/swiper-class.d.ts`. Follow the declaration adjacency at the file header, first confirm the object relationships, and then decide whether materials closer to the implementation are needed. The compatibility verification for R12.4 stops at this level on this page; do not infer callers that have not been established or execution results from the title or search terms.

# Record of Trade-offs in Preserving Release Automation State

This record initially framed the issue too much as page organization: where to put the cache, and where to put the return window. Only on reviewing it later did it become clear that what was truly at risk of being lost was not a particular passage of text, but whether the state left by a release could still be matched to the exit entry point. The original conclusion is therefore retained, but its conditions of applicability have been filled in.

The decision remains: do not rebuild the environment to complete this set of records, retain the current revision, and put the cache, original state, and exit actions that can be confirmed into a single traceable record. "Retain" here does not mean freezing all old values; after version synchronization, old values still exist as rollback entry points, but they are no longer treated as the current release state.

## Rebuilding the Environment Was Not Chosen at the Time

Version 1 included the idea of "separating out the return window". It came from a reasonable but incomplete expectation: a standalone page would be easier to maintain, and the cache could also be organized according to its own lifecycle. The issue raised during review was that a standalone page could only show what had been organized afterward, not which request or version a given exit action originally corresponded to, or why that record had stopped at the current revision.

Rebuilding the environment was also proposed. It could produce a tidier-looking set of pages and directories, but could not automatically recover the job from that time, the pages visible through the standard entry point, or the original requests whose associations had already been lost. The rebuilt result could easily be mistaken for the original state, especially when cache hits, version switching, and a rollback window occurred at the same time. Given this cost, the meeting did not adopt "rerunning to produce a clean environment" as a way to backfill the records.

This trade-off is therefore not about favoring the old entry point itself, but about avoiding replacing the original chain of connections with materials organized later. Content that can establish its provenance stays where it is; content that can only establish what was checked later is placed afterward as an addendum. The two types of material do not overwrite each other.

## Boundaries Left by the Previous Proposal

The old proposal has not been deleted, because it still explains why splitting the pages seemed desirable at the time: maintainers needed to view the return window separately, while cache records often changed with release actions. Mixing the two in long, unstructured paragraphs can indeed cause the person taking over to miss the window.

But the old proposal assumed that "splitting them apart and then linking them back together" would be enough. That assumption later ceased to apply. Access through the standard entry point was denied at the second step of the exit entry point, showing that being able to see a directory or the first-level page does not mean one can continue to the original request. If only the separate window page is left at that point, readers can see only that an exit action occurred; they cannot determine whether that action corresponds to an old value that is still available for rollback.

Another approach that was not adopted was to treat the cache as a separate version note, updated only after the release was complete. The problem was not whether the cache needed a version number, but that this would describe "the current value after the release" and "the old value retained for rollback" as the same type of state. The lag in version synchronization later recorded in SWPA-011 exposed exactly this issue: old values may continue to be retained as entry points, but this does not justify inferring that the current release has not changed.

An earlier judgment is retained here to make the context of version 1 easier to understand: at the time, it was thought that finding the current callers would be enough to determine where the cache records belonged. That judgment was not subsequently used as the basis for a final decision. Caller information helps with organizing pages, but cannot replace the correspondence among the original request, exit action, and rollback entry point.

## What Must Be Preserved This Time

The current revision is the anchor for this record. It is not synonymous with "the latest content must be correct", but rather the versioned state that the existing materials can still all point to. Three types of content are preserved around it:

1. Cache records: show what content was not erased when the pages were organized at the time, and which release cycle it still sits alongside.
2. Original state: preserve the locations of old entry points, screenshots, or page traces, without passing off an organized summary as the original request.
3. Exit actions: record the verified exit paths and their results. An exit action does not itself mean recovery is complete; if the original request is missing, all that can be noted is that the correspondence has not been established.

These three types of content are kept together without requiring every item to be complete. The current materials do, in fact, have gaps: in one place, only a screenshot remains, and the original request corresponding to the exit entry point has not been linked; in another check, access through the standard entry point could not continue past the second step. Leaving the gaps as they are in the relevant places is safer than adding a speculative connection on a new page.

The cache page also does not cover all release notes. It preserves only the parts directly adjacent to the current revision and the rollback window. Release notes, the maintainers' subsequent branches, and the consumers' three questions should each remain in their original materials; this page does not consolidate them into one master table. DOC-33 may continue to retain the questions raised by consumers, but must not be used to infer exit relationships that have not been confirmed here.

## What the Card Addenda Changed

Subsequent cards did not overturn the decision "not to rebuild the environment", but did change this record's requirements for what counts as "verifiable".

SWPA-008 first confirmed ownership of the exit actions, then adjusted who would continue handling them because the main work had shifted to modules · Release Automation Core Module. This change shows that exit actions are not just ownerless historical text; the verification path must be transferable to subsequent maintainers, but the handoff should not move the confirmed original state elsewhere. Actions and results remain on the page, while maintenance ownership continues to evolve through the cards.

After the handoff was confirmed in SWPA-005, the return window was no longer just a to-do item in the first version. The borrower, start time, and return window for the current revision need to be written back. However, this only resolves who has taken responsibility for the window; it does not automatically establish the actual consumers of the cache. The two matters cannot be conflated into a single judgment just because both are labeled "current revision".

When SWPA-011 was marked as blocked, the reason was that the previous night's job had expired and its logs were temporarily unavailable. The only material left afterward consisted of screenshots; the original request corresponding to the exit entry point still had not been linked. Here, screenshots are not elevated to substitutes for logs, nor are exit relationships guessed from page colors or filenames. When the original request is missing, the record should remain in the state of "exit entry point seen, original request not linked".

If no request or run ID has appeared yet, stop at the entry point and complete the record first; you cannot infer from this whether types-client-integration has already run.

Don't automatically mark the current revision as having run, either. Only include it in the same record as the observed behavior once you've confirmed that collection or execution actually took place; otherwise, leave it unknown. A response from the entry point or a message on the page does not mean the caller has reached downstream processing.

Previously, some people retried first, losing the first failing sample and the ability to compare environment differences. Now, record first, then decide whether to continue. A retry is not the default recovery action.

## Branches

**Rejected directly at the entry point, with no further indication of request/run**

Stay at the current entry point. Fill in the rejection location and identity, then hand off to the permissions maintainers. Don't route cases like this to types-client-integration: the existing record only shows that access was blocked at the entry point, not that the caller's type adaptation has started.

**There are indications of a request or run, but collection or execution is not yet confirmed**

Retain those clues and leave revision marked as unknown. The exit action here is to stop attributing a cause, not to clear records or reset state. Whoever takes over needs to first confirm what actually occurred—collection or execution. Until that is confirmed, don't continue down the type-issue path.

**The observed behavior now falls within the scope documented in types-client-integration**

Review the local nodes, starting from `docs/adj-types/runbooks/types-client-integration-blocked-escalation-contact.md`. First look for `module parameter`; it's a lookup term left in this record, not a confirmed cause. Once you find it, only match it to the location in the current failing sample; if it doesn't match, return to the entry-point sample. Don't invent a call chain.

If you then see `breakpoint migration`, don't clear the evidence. When this marker appears, you should retain both the first failing sample and the environment differences, especially the entry-point identity, whether there is already any indication of request/run, and whether revision has been confirmed. Older records treated this as a point where you could retry immediately, but afterward the rejection location could no longer be reproduced; that approach is no longer used.

**Further assessment is needed, but `controller peer` has not appeared**

Stop here. Don't conclude that this is a specific implementation defect just because module parameter or breakpoint migration appeared earlier. Without controller peer, this tree doesn't have enough evidence to go further; hand the retained sample, environment differences, and the point where you stopped back to types-client-integration, and wait for additional records.

## What to include in the handoff

When handing off to the permissions maintainers, describe the entry-point identity, the rejection location, and whether request/run is present. Without that information, they can only ask again what happened at the entry point and cannot determine whether the rejection came before integration processing.

When handing off to types-client-integration, include the first failing sample, environment differences, the module parameter lookup results, and whether controller peer appeared. Don't rewrite "access failure at the standard entry point" as "type definition failure"; the former may still be at the access layer, while the latter requires records showing that it reached the scope of integration testing.

If neither set of conditions is met, retain the exit action: record the current entry point, stop further attribution, and leave revision unknown. The recovery action has not yet been tried in the shared environment, so it cannot be treated as a verified step in this tree.

Related consumer issues can be found at DOC-41; this page only records where to stop when stuck and which side to hand off to.

# Team Public Entry Point Maintenance Mismatch

During the maintenance window, the result observed on site did not match the original plan. The entry page was still directing visitors to the old path, and the planned switchover was not reflected in what people saw. This was first spotted in a manual check after maintenance, not through an error reported in the execution record itself. The initial impact was on navigation: anyone who needed to access the team's public entry point would still see the old entry point, and we could not tell from the page alone whether the switchover was complete. There was no evidence that underlying content had been damaged, and the scope of impact was not extended to other projects.

## Timeline

- Window start: Worked on the public entry point according to the original plan, keeping the old entry point as a rollback point. This was considered a sufficient safeguard at the time.
- First check after maintenance: The visible result still did not match the plan. The page opened, but it pointed to a different entry point than expected.
- Initial assessment: On site, we initially thought this was just a viewer-side cache issue or a delayed page update, so we did not block it at the gate initially. That assessment did not fully hold up later; at the very least, the original execution record did not show that the visible entry point had been switched over.
- Temporary restoration: Put the old entry point back on a working path, making the team's public entry point usable during the shift again. This only restored access; it did not mean the cause of the mismatch had been found.
- Wrap-up check: Added the actual impact, coordinator, and rollback entry point to the record. At the time, the coordinator could only be tracked down through the maintenance-window contact; the original record did not include a consistent name or a dedicated escalation point.

## Original Execution Record

What we retained was the original execution record from the window; we did not rewrite it as proof that "the switchover was complete." The record supports two points: maintenance actions were performed, and the entry-point result was subsequently observed not to have caught up with the original plan. On its own, it cannot tell us whether the mismatch came from the release, the entry-point target, or the timing of the check. When we later revisited the file location, we searched using `src/types/modules/effect-cube.d.ts` and the call name, but that was only where the search led at the time, not enough to attribute this organizational coordination issue to a source file. The old assessment is retained here: at the time, we attributed the visible mismatch mainly to entry-point update timing; until the missing cross-check of the environment and execution records is complete, that attribution should not be treated as confirmed fact.

## Impact and Open Issues

Confirmed: one entry-point mismatch during the window, and reliance on the old entry point for temporary restoration. Unconfirmed: why the original plan was not reflected in the visible result, how long the old entry point was actually accessed, and whether any visitors took the wrong path as a result. If we handle a similar window again, first record the actual visible result, coordinator, and rollback entry point, then decide whether to let it through; do not judge maintenance complete just because "the page opens."

# Shared Entry Point Maintenance FAQ

This page was often treated as closure guidance for the shared entry point, but it is actually just a set of questions and answers left over from several rounds of maintenance. The wording about the entry point maintainer from the first two versions is still here to help explain why people handed candidate paths directly to them at the time; it is not a verified division of responsibilities.

Here, "shared" only describes a lookup location used by multiple people. It does not mean the entry point establishes the same conclusion for every consumer. When the entry point is retained, maintenance can continue around it; whether behavior is consistent still needs a separate check. The old page conflated these two layers, making a name read like a completion marker.

**What does the existing virtual-framework entry point establish?**

It establishes that the shared path still points to virtual-framework, making it a suitable place to start looking. It does not establish that framework consumers have passed, or that the DOM side and the paths adjacent to loop are unchanged. The earlier wording equated "the entry point is still there" with "compatibility is in place"; that conclusion was too broad. This review corrects that point only; it does not supply execution results for the individual consumers.

Nor does the entry point's name establish that any specific consumer ever carried out a review. It only points to a candidate relationship: when confirmation is needed, continue from there to check the target behavior and the regression path immediately next to it. Do not fill in a pass here for consumers with no records, or mark them as failed just because no records were found. The entry point can narrow the search, but it is not a substitute for execution results.

**Who withdraws a candidate path?**

The party that proposed the candidate path is responsible for first withdrawing their own candidate content; the shared entry point maintainer is responsible for removing or rewriting the reference in the entry point. If they are the same person, both actions can be taken together, but that does not mean all withdrawal work falls under entry point maintenance. Past items for which the original execution records were not retained can be logged, but logging them only establishes that someone raised a question, not whether the actual withdrawal was completed.

Withdrawal often involves two changes that appear connected but have different records: the candidate content itself disappears, and the entry point's mention of it is deleted or rewritten. If the former has not happened, changes to the entry point text cannot substitute for withdrawal; if the latter has not happened, there is no basis to say the shared documentation has caught up either. The old log entries lack original execution records, so they cannot be used to backfill the order of the two actions. Nor can the entry point's continued presence or its having been rewritten establish who completed which step.

**What are the conditions for closure?**

The wording the team used at the time was: Close compatibility work only after the target behavior and neighboring regression path agree across the relevant DOM, loop, and framework consumers.

This is stricter than "close once the target behavior can be reproduced," and explains why the previous version could not close the work based solely on the virtual-framework entry point. Here, the neighboring regression path refers to the DOM, loop, and framework consumers adjacent to the same compatibility assessment; it is not a requirement to recheck every shared entry point.

The word agree in that sentence does not mean merely getting a result once on one side; it puts target behavior and neighboring regression path in the same closure decision and limits the scope to relevant DOM, loop, and framework consumers. The simplified closure criterion used at the time was therefore no longer sufficient, but it was still retained in the previous version and cannot be treated as current confirmation. The available material does not include the original execution records for each consumer, so it cannot establish that any particular closure met all the conditions.

If the question is only whether the entry point still exists, the answer can be that it still points to the candidate relationship. If the question becomes whether a particular consumer has passed, or whether a particular withdrawal is complete, the available material only supports marking that as unknown. Do not infer either type of result from the existence of the shared entry point.

Still unconfirmed: whether the old log entries lacking original execution records actually covered the corresponding framework consumers. This page has no material that answers that.
